metadata.title: Minimal degree equations for curves and surfaces (variations on a theme of Halphen)

nodes.name: Setting: integral $m$-dimensional $X\subset \mathbb P^n$ with $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s-1))=0$
nodes.statement: To introduce the problem, let $X$ be an $m$-dimensional integral projective variety in $\mathbb P^n$. Let $s$ be an integer with the property that $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree strictly smaller than $s$, i.e., $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s-1))=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Standing setup: an integral $m$-dimensional $X\subset\mathbb P^n$ lying on no hypersurface of degree $<s$.

nodes.name: Question on the minimal degree of such an $X$
nodes.statement: What is the minimal degree that such an $X$ may have?

nodes.name: Question on how big $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$ may be
nodes.statement: For such a projective variety $X$, how big $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$ may be?

nodes.name: Park's Problem A
nodes.statement: Park \cite[Problem A]{park} posed the problem of determining the maximal possible values of $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$, for every $s$ without further assumptions
nodes.statement_short: Determine the maximal possible $h^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$ for every $s$, with no extra hypotheses.

nodes.name: $k$-normality of a projective variety
nodes.statement: another line of research investigates the $k$-normality of a projective variety, i.e., the objective is to find out the least integer $k$ such that the system of degree $k$ hypersurfaces of the ambient projective space cut out a complete linear system on $X$
nodes.origin_citation: Gruson, Lazarsfeld & Peskine 1983; Lazarsfeld 1987; Alzati & Russo
differentia: the system of degree $k$ hypersurfaces of the ambient projective space cut out a complete linear system on $X$

nodes.name: Varieties of almost-minimal degree
nodes.statement: Furthermore, Park's extremal cases are related to the study of varieties $X\subset \PP^n$ of almost-minimal degree, i.e., $\deg(X)=\textnormal{codim}(X)+2$
nodes.origin_citation: Brodmann & Schenzel 2007; Fujisawa 1995; Park 2007; Hoa, Stückrad & Vogel 1991

nodes.name: The collection $\Aa (n,s,m)$
nodes.statement: Let $m \ge 1$, $s\ge 3$ and $n\ge m+2$. Define \[ \Aa (n,s,m) = \left\lbrace \mbox{integral $m$-dimensional } X\subset \PP^n \ | \ h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0 \right\rbrace. \]
nodes.statement_short: $\Aa(n,s,m)$ collects the integral $m$-dimensional $X\subset\PP^n$ lying on no degree $s-1$ hypersurface.

nodes.name: Members of $\Aa (n,s,m)$ are non-degenerate
nodes.statement: Since $s>1$, any $X\in \Aa (n,s,m)$ is non-degenerate, i.e., it spans the ambient projective space, as one clearly has $h^0(\Ii_X(1)) = 0$.
conclusions: any $X\in \Aa (n,s,m)$ is non-degenerate, i.e., it spans the ambient projective space

nodes.name: The minimal degree $d_{n,s,m}$
nodes.statement: We introduce two numerical invariants: \[ d_{n,s,m} = \min \left\lbrace \deg(X) \ | \ X\in \Aa (n,s,m) \right\rbrace, \mbox{ and } \]

nodes.name: The invariant $\alpha (n,s,m)$
nodes.statement: \[ \alpha (n,s,m) = \max \left\lbrace h^0(\Ii _X(s)) \ | \ X\in \Aa(n,s,m) \right\rbrace. \] Hence $\alpha(n,s,m)$ is the maximal number, over the set $\Aa(n,s,m)$, of the linearly independent hypersurfaces of degree $s$ vanishing on some $X\in \Aa(n,s,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha(n,s,m)$ is the maximal number of independent degree $s$ hypersurfaces through a member of $\Aa(n,s,m)$.

nodes.name: Coning down: $d_{n,s,m} \le d_{n-1,s,m-1}$
nodes.statement: For $m\ge 2$, we have $d_{n,s,m} \le d_{n-1,s, m-1}$. To see this, take $X\subset \mathbb P^{n-1}$ of dimension $m-1$ with minimal degree $\deg(X)=d_{n-1,s,m-1}$. Let $C(X)$ be the cone over $X$ with a single point as vertex: this sits in $\PP^n$, it has dimension $m$ and degree $d_{n-1,s,m-1}$. Moreover, it is clear that $C(X)\in \Aa(n,s,m)$.
nodes.statement_short: Taking a cone over a minimal degree $(m-1)$-fold gives $d_{n,s,m}\le d_{n-1,s,m-1}$ for $m\ge2$.

nodes.name: Curve-case notation $\Aa (n,s)$, $d_{n,s}$, $\alpha (n,s)$
nodes.statement: For the ease of notation, we set \[ \Aa (n,s):= \Aa (n,s,1), d_{n,s}:= d_{n,s,1}, \mbox{ and } \alpha (n,s):= \alpha (n,s,1). \]

nodes.name: The family $H(d,g;n)$
nodes.statement: We introduce another piece of notation: \[ H(d,g;n) = \left\lbrace \mbox{smooth, connected, non-deg. } X\subset \PP^n, \deg(X) = d, p_a(X) = g\right\rbrace. \]

nodes.name: The family $H(d,g;n)'$
nodes.statement: In the range of degree $d\ge g+1$, define \[ H(d,g;n)' = \left\lbrace X\in H(d,g;n)\ | \ h^1(\Oo _X(1)) =0\right\rbrace. \] Note that $H(d,g; n)'=H(d,g; n)$ whenever $d>2g-2$, as $\Oo_X(1)$ is non-special.
nodes.statement_short: $H(d,g;n)'$ is the subfamily of $H(d,g;n)$ with non-special hyperplane bundle.

nodes.name: Value of the minimal degree $d_{n,s}$ of curves
nodes.statement: The numerical invariant $d_{n,s}$ satisfies \[ d_{n,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \]
nodes.statement_short: The minimal degree of a curve on no degree $s-1$ hypersurface of $\PP^n$ is $\lceil(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1)/(s-1)\rceil$.
assumptions: In this section, we focus on the case of curves, i.e., $m=1$.

nodes.name: Proof of the value of $d_{n,s}$
nodes.statement: Let \[ \delta = \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \] We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$. For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \PP^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\Ii _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \NN$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\Oo_{\PP^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}. Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$. For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \PP^n$ such that $h^0(\Ii _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\Ii _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\Oo _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give \[ h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1, \] for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$. Thus \[ \deg(\Oo_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\Oo_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Double inequality: general maximal-rank rational curves give $d_{n,s}\le\delta$, and $h^0(L)\le\deg(L)+1$ gives $d_{n,s}\ge\delta$.

nodes.name: Maximal rank of the general smooth rational curve in $H(d,0;n)$
nodes.statement: the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \PP^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\Ii _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \NN$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\Oo_{\PP^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}.
nodes.statement_short: The general degree $d$ rational curve in $\PP^n$ has maximal rank, so $h^0(\Ii_X(t))=0$ exactly when numerically possible.

nodes.name: Arithmetic genus bound for minimal degree curves in $\Aa(n,s)$
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be an integral curve $X\in \Aa(n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d_{n,s}$. Then its arithmetic genus satisfies \[ p_a(X) \le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: A minimal degree curve in $\Aa(n,s)$ has $p_a(X)\le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$.
assumptions: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be an integral curve $X\in \Aa(n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d_{n,s}$

nodes.name: Proof of the arithmetic genus bound
nodes.statement: Since $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$. Otherwise, assume $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\Oo _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch settles the non-special case; otherwise Clifford's theorem plus the value of $d_{n,s}$ contradicts $s\ge3$.

nodes.name: Genus range, the Claim $s-2\le d_{n,s}-n$, and $h^0(\Ii_X(s))$ for $g=g_0$
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $g$ such that $0\le g \le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Again, as in the proof of Lemma \ref{i2}, Proposition \ref{i1} yields \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}, \] and so $g\le s-2$. \begin{quote} {\it Claim.} We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.\\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show \[ (s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Let $\phi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider \[ \phi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2. \] It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: \[ \phi (n+1,s) -\phi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \ s\ge 3, \] which leads to a contradiction. \end{quote} By the {\it Claim} and \cite{be2, be3}, a general curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)'$ has maximal rank. Moreover, for each integer $g$ with $0\le g\le (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, there exists a curve $X\in H(d_{n,s},g;n)$ such that $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$. Since $h^1(\Oo _X(1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\omega_X(-1)) = 0$. The latter condition is equivalent to $h^0(\omega_X(-t))=0$ for all $t\geq 1$. Hence $h^1(\Oo _X(t)) =0$ for $t=s-1,s$. Moreover, we have: \[ h^1(\Ii _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d_{n,s}+1-g -\binom{n+s-1}{n}, \] \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s)) = h^1(\Ii _X(s)) +\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g. \] Now, choose $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, so that $h^1(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$. Furthermore \[ h^2(\Ii _X(s-2)) =h^1(\Oo _X(s-2)) =0, \] where the right-most equality holds because $s\ge3$. By the well-known Castelnuovo-Mumford's Lemma, we derive \[h^1(\Ii _X(t)) =0 \mbox{ for all } t\ge s. \] Finally, \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd_{n,s}-1+g_0 = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Shows $g\le s-2$ and $s-2\le d_{n,s}-n$, then computes $h^0(\Ii_X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}$ for the extremal genus $g_0$.

nodes.name: Claim: $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$
nodes.statement: We have $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Claim $s-2 \le d_{n,s}-n$
nodes.statement: By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show \[ (s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Let $\phi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range. Indeed, consider \[ \phi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2. \] It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$. Moreover: \[ \phi (n+1,s) -\phi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \ s\ge 3, \] which leads to a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: the auxiliary function $\phi(n,s)$ is non-negative, checked at $n=3$ and by its increments in $n$.

nodes.name: Summary: $d_{n,s}\ge n+g_0$ and $h^0(\Ii_X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}$
nodes.statement: Setting $g_0 = (s-1)d_{n,s} + 1 -\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, We have: \[ d_{n,s} \ge n+g_0; \] additionally, a general curve $X\in H(d,g_0;n)'$ satisfies \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0 \mbox{ and } h^0(\Ii _X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Summary of the previous remark: the extremal genus $g_0$ satisfies $d_{n,s}\ge n+g_0$ and realizes $h^0(\Ii_X(s))=\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-d_{n,s}$.

nodes.name: Question: is $\alpha (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}$?
nodes.statement: Is it true that \[ \alpha (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d_{n,s}? \] Keep the definition of $g_0$ from Remark \ref{observation}. Does equality hold if and only if $X$ is a general curve in $H(d_{n,s}, g_0; n)'$?

nodes.name: Formula for $h^0(\Ii _X(s))$ of a curve with $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 3$ and $s\ge3$. Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate curve such that $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) = 0$. Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \PP^n$. Then \begin{align} & h^0(\Ii _X(s)) = \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X) -h^1(\Ii_X(s-1)) + h^1(\Ii _X(s))+ \\ & \nonumber \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ + h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) -h^1(\Oo _X(s)). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Exact bookkeeping formula for $h^0(\Ii_X(s))$ in terms of $\deg X$ and the $h^1$'s of $\Ii_X$ and $\Oo_X$.
assumptions: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate curve such that $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) = 0$.

nodes.name: Proof of the formula for $h^0(\Ii _X(s))$
nodes.statement: Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \PP^n$. Note that $h^0(H,\Ii _{X\cap H}(s)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X)+h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H}(s))$. Since $h^1(\Oo _X(t)) =h^2(\Ii _X(t))$ for all $t\in \mathbb Z$, in order to conclude it is sufficient to use the long exact sequence in cohomology of the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0\to \Ii _X(s-1)\to \Ii _X(s)\to \Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0, \end{equation} along with the assumption $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: Count sections on a general hyperplane, then run the long exact cohomology sequence of the hyperplane restriction sequence.

nodes.name: The numerical function $\psi (t)$
nodes.statement: Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\Oo _X(t-1)) -h^1(\Oo _X(t))$.

nodes.name: The Castelnuovo invariant $\chi$
nodes.statement: As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$.

nodes.name: Castelnuovo's vanishing and monotonicity beyond $\chi$
nodes.statement: As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\Oo _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}. Furthermore, $h^1(\Ii _X(t)) \ge h^1(\Ii _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, and $h^1(\Ii _X(t))> h^1(\Ii _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\Ii _X(t))\ne 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Past $\chi$ the groups $h^1(\Oo_X(t))$ vanish and $h^1(\Ii_X(t))$ is (strictly) decreasing.
nodes.origin_citation: Castelnuovo; Szpiro 1979, Theorem 1 p.52 and Lemma 2 p.53

nodes.name: Discussion of the right-hand side of the $h^0(\Ii _X(s))$ formula
nodes.statement: In the setting of Lemma \ref{i00+}, as usual let $d = \deg (X)$ and $g = p_a(X)$. Since $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$, by Riemann-Roch, we have \[ h^1(\Ii _X(s-1)) = (s-1)d +1-g-\binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Define the numerical function $\psi (t) := h^1(\Oo _X(t-1)) -h^1(\Oo _X(t))$. For fixed integers $g$, $h^1(\Ii _X(s))$ and $\psi(s)$, the right-hand side of (\ref{eqi00+}) is a strictly decreasing function in $d$. Since $\deg (\Oo _X(t)) =d+\deg (\Oo _X(t-1))$, Serre duality and Riemann-Roch give \[ 0\le \psi (t) \le d. \] Therefore a class of curves for which the term $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) -h^1(\Oo _X(s))$ is zero is realized when $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$. Moreover, note that the long exact sequence in cohomology of (\ref{eqi01}) yields \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s)) \le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1} -d, \] whenever $h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s)) =0$. As in \cite[Chapter 3]{szp}, let $\chi$ denote the minimal non-negative integer such that $h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(\chi +1)) =0$. As classically shown by Castelnuovo, using (\ref{eqi01}) one obtains $h^1(\Oo _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Theorem 1, p. 52]{szp}. Furthermore, $h^1(\Ii _X(t)) \ge h^1(\Ii _X(t+1))$ for all $t\ge \chi$ \cite[Lemma 2, p. 53]{szp}, and $h^1(\Ii _X(t))> h^1(\Ii _X(t+1))$ whenever $t>\chi$ and $h^1(\Ii _X(t))\ne 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The formula's right-hand side decreases in $d$; $0\le\psi(t)\le d$, and Castelnuovo's $\chi$ controls the remaining $h^1$ terms.

nodes.name: Question: existence of curves of degree $d>d_{n,s}$ with $h^0(\Ii _X(s))\ne 0$
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$ and $d> d_{n,s}$. \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] Is there an integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \PP^n$ such that $\deg (X)=d$, $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s))\ne 0$? \item[(ii)] Can we choose such an $X$ to be smooth? \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: The four Halphen ranges of pairs $(d,s)$ in $\PP^3$
nodes.statement: Recall that, by Proposition \ref{i1}, \[ d_{3,s} = \left\lceil \left(\binom{s+2}{3}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \] For $d, s\ge 3$, to each pair $(d,s)$, we attach the set of degree $d$ curves in $\PP^3$ {\it not} contained in any surface of degree $<s$. Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair. It is customary to divide the set of pairs $(d,s)$ into four regions:
nodes.statement_short: Sets up the classical partition of pairs $(d,s)$ into Ranges $\emptyset$, A, B, C for space curves.

nodes.name: Halphen's question
nodes.statement: Given $(d,s)$, Halphen's question asks in particular to determine the maximum genus of a curve associated to this pair.

nodes.name: Range $\emptyset$: no space curve exists
nodes.statement: {\bf Range $\emptyset$}: $d < (s^2+4s+6)/6 $. In this range, there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \PP^3$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$ \cite[Theorem 3.3]{h0}, \cite{hh}.
conclusions: there is no integral and non-degenerate curve $X\subset \PP^3$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$

nodes.name: Range A: existence of space curves and maximal genera
nodes.statement: {\bf Range A}: $(s^2+4s+6)/6 \le d < (s^2+4s+6)/3$. In this range, one finds curves with $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\Oo _X(s))=0$. Thus if $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s)) \ne 0$, by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g \ge \binom{s+2}{3}$ and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$. Moreover, if $\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil \le d <(s^2+4s+6)/3$, it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed; see, e.g., \cite{bbem, fl1,fl2}. To fill in all $(d,s)$ such that $(s^2+4s+6)/6\le d < \lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ the same result (the existence of curves with $(d,s)$ and $g= (s-1)d+1- \binom{s+2}{3}$) is only known for $s$ large enough, i.e., $s \geq 10.5\times 10^5$, by the recent \cite[Theorem 1]{be6}.
nodes.statement_short: In Range A curves with $h^1(\Oo_X(s-1))=0$ exist and attain the maximal genus, fully for $d\ge\lceil s(s+2)/4\rceil$ and otherwise only for huge $s$.
nodes.origin_citation: Ballico, Bolondi, Ellia & Miró-Roig 1997; Fløystad 1991; Ballico & Ellia 2018, Theorem 1
conclusions: In this range, one finds curves with $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^1(\Oo _X(s))=0$
it is known such a curve exists for any such choice of $(d,s)$, along with curves reaching the maximal genera allowed

nodes.name: Hartshorne--Hirschowitz maximal genus conjecture in Range B
nodes.statement: {\bf Range B}: $(s^2+4s+6)/3\le d < s(s-1)$. Hartshorne and Hirschowitz constructed, for any $(d, s)$ in this range, smooth space curves with very high genera and conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$ \cite{hh, ms}.
nodes.statement_short: The Hartshorne--Hirschowitz curves are conjectured to have maximal genus throughout Range B.
conclusions: conjectured that they have the maximal genus for all curves associated to $(d,s)$

nodes.name: Range C: Gruson--Peskine classification of maximal genus curves
nodes.statement: {\bf Range C}: $d>s(s-1)$. One finds a smooth degree $d$ space curve $X$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$; Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus \cite{gp1}: if $d\equiv 0\pmod{s}$, these curves are complete intersections of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $d/s$; in all other cases $X$ is {\it linked} to a plane curve $C$ of degree $\deg(C) = s\lceil d/s\rceil -d$, by the complete intersection of a surface of degree $s$ and a surface of degree $\lceil d/s\rceil$. For $d\geq s^2$, we have $h^0(\Ii _X(s)) \le 2$ with equality if and only if $d=s^2$ and $X$ is the complete intersection of two surfaces of degree $s$.
nodes.statement_short: In Range C maximal genus curves are complete intersections or linked to a plane curve, and $h^0(\Ii_X(s))\le2$ for $d\ge s^2$.
conclusions: Gruson and Peskine classified all such curves $X$ of maximal genus
For $d\geq s^2$, we have $h^0(\Ii _X(s)) \le 2$ with equality if and only if $d=s^2$ and $X$ is the complete intersection of two surfaces of degree $s$

nodes.name: Cohomology of the known Range A curves
nodes.statement: Assume $(d,s)$ is in {\bf Range A}. Let $X\subset \PP^3$ be any integral curve with $\deg (X)=d$, $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$, $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$, and $h^0(\Ii _X(s)) \ne 0$, i.e., by Riemann-Roch one has $(s-1)d+1-g\ge \binom{s+2}{3}$, and $sd+1-g\le \binom{s+3}{3}$, where $g = p_a(X)$ is the arithmetic genus of $X$. All curves constructed in \cite{bbem, be6, bef, fl1, fl2} have $h^1(\Ii _X(s-1)) = h^2(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$ and hence $h^0(\Ii _X(s)) =\binom{s+2}{2} - d$. The ones in the main results of \cite{bbem, be6} have $g= d(s-1)+1-\binom{s+2}{3}$, whereas the ones given in \cite[Proposition 4.3]{bbem} and in \cite{bef} have many different genera for the fixed pair $(d,s)$.
nodes.statement_short: All known Range A constructions satisfy $h^1(\Ii_X(s-1))=h^2(\Ii_X(s-1))=0$, so $h^0(\Ii_X(s))=\binom{s+2}{2}-d$.

nodes.name: The families $\Bb (n,s,d)$ and $\Bb (n,s,d)'$
nodes.statement: We generalize {\bf Range A} to curves embedded in $\PP^n$ for any $n\geq 3$. For all integers $n\geq 3$, $s\ge 2$ and $d\ge d_{n,s}$, let $\Bb (n,s,d)$ (resp. $\Bb (n,s,d)'$) denote the set of all smooth and connected (resp. integral) $X\in \Aa (n,s)$ such that $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Bb(n,s,d)$ collects the degree $d$ members of $\Aa(n,s)$ with $h^1(\Oo_X(s-1))=0$.

nodes.name: Generalized Range A
nodes.statement: Curves in $\Bb (n,s,d)$ are said to be in the {\it generalized} {\bf Range A}.

nodes.name: Genus bound for curves in $\Bb (n,s,d)'$
nodes.statement: Let $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)'$. Since $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$, Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\Oo _X(s-1)) =d(s-1)+1-p_a(X)$. Since $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$, one obtains $h^0(\Oo _X(s-1))\geq h^0(\Oo _{\PP^n}(s-1)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n}$, and so: \[ p_a(X)\le d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Curves in the generalized Range A satisfy $p_a(X)\le d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$.

nodes.name: Questions on maximal genus in the generalized Range A
nodes.statement: We pose the following questions: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] For which choices of $d, s, n$, does there exist $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)$ (or even $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)'$) such that $p_a(X) =d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$? \item[(ii)] What is the maximal arithmetic genus of curves in $\Bb (n,s,d)$ (or in $\Bb (n,s,d)'$)? \item[(iii)] For which $g_0$ and every $0\le g \le g_0$, does there exist $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)$ (or $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)'$) with such arithmetic genus? \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Extremal curves in $\Bb (n,s,d)'$ and ideal generation
nodes.statement: For any $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)'$, one has $h^2(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$. Suppose there exists $X\in \Bb (n,s,d)'$ such that $p_a(X) =d(s-1)+1-\binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Thus $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) = h^2(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$. By Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\Oo _X(s-1))=0$, and hence $h^1(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$. Therefore, these curves are exactly the integral and non-degenerate degree $d$ curves $X\subset \PP^n$ such that $h^i(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$ for all $i\ge 0$; this is because for any curve $Y\subset \PP^n$, one has $h^i(\Ii_Y(t)) =h^{i+1}(\Oo _{\PP^n}(t))=0$ for all $i\ge 3, i\neq n$ and all $t\in \ZZ$, and for all $t>-n$ when $i=n$. Take any hyperplane $H\subset \PP^n$. By the exact sequence (\ref{eqi01}), we have $h^1(\Ii _X(s)) = h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s))$. Assume $h^1(\Oo _X(s-2))=0$, i.e., $h^1(\Ii _X(s-2))=0$. Since $h^i(\Ii _X(t)) =0$ for all $i\ge 3$ and $t> -n$, we have $h^i(\Ii _X(s-1-i)) =0$ for all $i\ge 0$. In this case, Castelnuovo-Mumford's lemma gives $h^1(\Ii _X(t)) =0$ for all $t\ge s$: this implies that the homogeneous ideal of $X$ is generated by $\textnormal{H}^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$. Now we drop the assumption $h^1(\Oo _X(s-2))=0$, and instead suppose $h^1(\Ii _X(s)) =0$, i.e., $h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s))=0$. This implies $d\le \binom{n+s-1}{n-1}$. In this case, the Castelnuovo-Mumford's lemma gives $h^1(\Ii _X(t)) =0$ for all $t>s$, which implies that the homogeneous ideal of $X$ is generated by $\textnormal{H}^0(\mathcal I_X(s))$ and $\textnormal{H}^0(\mathcal I_X(s+1))$.
nodes.statement_short: Extremal generalized Range A curves have all $h^i(\Ii_X(s-1))=0$, and Castelnuovo-Mumford then bounds the degrees generating their homogeneous ideal.

nodes.name: Numerical range where Question on $d>d_{n,s}$ has a positive answer
nodes.statement: Fix integers $n, d, g, s$ such that $n\ge 3$, $s\ge 3$, with \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $0 \le g \le d-n$, \item[(ii)] $(n+1)d \ge ng +n(n+1)$, \item[(iii)] $(s-1)d \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n} +g-1$, and \item[(iv)] $sd \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}+g-2$. \end{enumerate} By results shown in \cite{be2, be4, be5}, there exists a smooth, connected, and non-degenerate {\it maximal rank} curve $X\subset \PP^n$ with $\deg (X) = d$, arithmetic genus $p_a(X)=g$, and $h^0(\Ii _X(s)) =\binom{n+s}{n} -sd+g-1$. Hence, setting the arithmetic genus to be the maximal in this range, i.e., $g=d-n$, (i) and (ii) in Question \ref{xq1} have a positive answer, whenever \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s))>0 \Longleftrightarrow (s-1)d < \binom{n+s}{n} -n-1. \] Note that inequality (iii) implies $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) = 0$, because $X$ has maximal rank.
nodes.statement_short: Known maximal rank curves give an affirmative answer to the smoothness question whenever $(s-1)d<\binom{n+s}{n}-n-1$.

nodes.name: The $\PP^m$-bundle $T = \PP(\Ee)$ and the minimal degree cone $W$
nodes.statement: Let $m \ge 1$ and $e\ge 2$. Consider the rank $m+1$ vector bundle $\Ee = \Oo _{\PP^1}\oplus \Oo _{\PP^1}(-e)^{\oplus m}$ on $\PP^1$. Define the corresponding projective bundle $T = \PP(\Ee)$ and let $\pi: T\to \PP^1$ be the vector bundle projection on $\PP^1$. The map $\pi$ makes $T$ a $\PP^{m}$-bundle and hence $\mathrm{Pic}(T) \cong \ZZ^2$, with basis given by a fiber $f$ of $\pi$ and any line bundle on $T$ whose restriction to any fiber of $\pi$ has degree one; see, e.g., \cite[Ex. II.7.9]{h}. Among these generators we take the only one, say $h$, such that $|h| =\{h\}$ (this corresponds to the unique surjection $\Oo _{\PP^1}\oplus \Oo _{\PP^1}(-e)^{\oplus m} \to \Oo _{\PP^1}$, \cite[Ch. II]{h}). As an abstract variety, $h$ is the trivial $\PP^{m-1}$-bundle over $\PP^1$ and hence $h\cong \PP^1\times \PP^{m-1}$. Similarly to the case of surfaces \cite[Ch. V]{h}, for any $a, b\in\ZZ$ we have $|ah+bf|\ne\emptyset$ if and only if either $a=0$ and $b\ge 0$ or $a>0$ and $b\ge ae$. The line bundle $\Oo_T(ah+bf)$ is globally generated (resp. ample) if and only if $a\ge 0$ and $b\ge ae$ (resp. $a>0$ and $b>ae$). The complete linear system $h+ef$ induces a morphism $u: T\to \PP^n$, where $n = e+m$, as $h^0(\Oo _{\PP^1}(e)\oplus \Oo _{\PP^1}^{\oplus m}) =e+1+m$. Let $W= u(T)$ be the image of $T$. The morphism $u$ contracts $h$ to an $(m-1)$-dimensional linear space in $\PP^r$, whereas $u|_{T\setminus h}$ is an embedding. Thus $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, as the support of $h$ is codimension-one. \begin{quote} {\it Claim.} The variety $W$ has degree $e$. \\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} Since $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, $\deg (W)= (h+ef)^{m+1}$, where the latter integer is the intersection product in the Chow ring of $T$ of $m+1$ copies of the divisor $h+ef$ defining the morphism. Since any two different fibers of $\pi$ are disjoint, the class $f^2$ in the Chow ring is zero. Thus $(h+ef)^{m+1} = h^{m+1} +(m+1)eh^mf$. Fix a fiber $F\in |f|$ of $\pi$. Since $h_{|F}$ is the degree one line bundle on $F$ and $F\cong \PP^{m}$, we have $h^{m}f =1$ and hence $(m+1)eh^{m}f =(m+1)e$. \\ If $m=1$, $T$ is a rational ruled surface. The normal bundle of $h$ has degree $h^2=-e$. Hence the conclusion follows for $m=1$. \\ Assume $m\ge 2$. Since $h \cong \PP^1\times \PP^{m-1}$, we have $\mathrm{Pic}(h)\cong \ZZ^2$. As generators of the lattice $\mathrm{Pic}(h)$, we take the pullbacks of hyperplane classes of the factors through the projections $\pi _1: h\to \PP^1$ and $\pi _2: h\to \PP^{m-1}$, i.e., $\Oo _h(1,0) = \pi _1^\ast (\Oo_{\PP^1}(1))$ and $\Oo _h(0,1) = \pi _2^\ast (\Oo _{\PP^{m-1}}(1))$. \\ By definition, the restriction $h_{|h}$ is the normal bundle of $h$ in $T$ and hence $h_{|h} \cong \Oo _h(-e,1)$, by induction on $m$ and using standard exact sequences on normal bundles. Thus $h^{m+1} = h^m|_{h} = -me$, concluding the proof. \end{quote} By this {\it Claim}, $W$ is a minimal degree $(m+1)$-dimensional subvariety of $\PP^{n}$, where $n=e+m$. It is a cone whose vertex is the $(m-1)$-dimensional linear space $V= u(h)$, and the base of the cone is a rational normal curve in any linear space $M\subset \PP^n$ such that $\dim M = n-m = e$ and $M\cap V=\emptyset$. Thus $W$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay. In particular, for any integer $s>0$, a divisor $X\subset W$ is contained in a degree $s$ hypersurface of $\PP^n$ if and only if its pullback $X'$ to $T$ is a part of the linear system $|sh+sef|$, i.e., there exists a divisor $X''\ge 0$ such that $X'+X'' \in |sh+sef|$. Thus $X$ is not contained in any degree $s$ hypersurface of $\PP^n$ if $X'\in |h+bf|$ for some integer $b \geq se+1$. In the Chow ring, we have: \[\deg (X) =X'\cdot (h+ef)^m = (h+bf)\cdot(h+ef)^m = \] \[ =h^{m+1}+meh^{m}f+b = b. \]
nodes.statement_short: Builds the $\PP^m$-bundle $T=\PP(\Oo\oplus\Oo(-e)^{\oplus m})$, shows its image $W$ under $|h+ef|$ is a minimal degree cone of degree $e$, and computes $\deg X=b$ for divisors $X'\in|h+bf|$.

nodes.name: Claim: the variety $W$ has degree $e$
nodes.statement: The variety $W$ has degree $e$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Claim that $\deg W = e$
nodes.statement: Since $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, $\deg (W)= (h+ef)^{m+1}$, where the latter integer is the intersection product in the Chow ring of $T$ of $m+1$ copies of the divisor $h+ef$ defining the morphism. Since any two different fibers of $\pi$ are disjoint, the class $f^2$ in the Chow ring is zero. Thus $(h+ef)^{m+1} = h^{m+1} +(m+1)eh^mf$. Fix a fiber $F\in |f|$ of $\pi$. Since $h_{|F}$ is the degree one line bundle on $F$ and $F\cong \PP^{m}$, we have $h^{m}f =1$ and hence $(m+1)eh^{m}f =(m+1)e$. If $m=1$, $T$ is a rational ruled surface. The normal bundle of $h$ has degree $h^2=-e$. Hence the conclusion follows for $m=1$. Assume $m\ge 2$. Since $h \cong \PP^1\times \PP^{m-1}$, we have $\mathrm{Pic}(h)\cong \ZZ^2$. As generators of the lattice $\mathrm{Pic}(h)$, we take the pullbacks of hyperplane classes of the factors through the projections $\pi _1: h\to \PP^1$ and $\pi _2: h\to \PP^{m-1}$, i.e., $\Oo _h(1,0) = \pi _1^\ast (\Oo_{\PP^1}(1))$ and $\Oo _h(0,1) = \pi _2^\ast (\Oo _{\PP^{m-1}}(1))$. By definition, the restriction $h_{|h}$ is the normal bundle of $h$ in $T$ and hence $h_{|h} \cong \Oo _h(-e,1)$, by induction on $m$ and using standard exact sequences on normal bundles. Thus $h^{m+1} = h^m|_{h} = -me$, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Expand $(h+ef)^{m+1}$ in the Chow ring using $f^2=0$, $h^mf=1$ and the normal bundle $h_{|h}\cong\Oo_h(-e,1)$.

nodes.name: Non-cone varieties of arbitrarily high degree in $\Aa(n,s,m)$
nodes.statement: Let $m\ge 1$, $n\ge m+3$, $s\ge 3$ and $d\ge (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$. There exists an integral and non-degenerate $m$-dimensional variety $X\subset \PP^n$, with $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$. Moreover, $X$ is not a cone.
nodes.statement_short: For $d\ge (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$ there is an $m$-dimensional non-cone $X\in\Aa(n,s,m)$ of degree $d$.
conclusions: There exists an integral and non-degenerate $m$-dimensional variety $X\subset \PP^n$, with $\deg (X)=d$ and $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$.

nodes.name: Proof of the existence of non-cone varieties in $\Aa(n,s,m)$
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \PP^n$ be a linear subspace with $\dim H = n-m$. Take a linear subspace $E\subset \PP^n$ such that $\dim E =m-1$ and $E\cap H=\emptyset$. By \cite{hi, be2} (for the case $n=4$), \cite{be2} (for the case $n=5$) and \cite{be3} (for the case $n\ge 6$), there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that \[ \deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}. \] Let $W'$ be the cone with vertex $E$ and such a curve $Y\subset H$ as its base. Up to a projective transformation, the projective variety depends only on $Y$, and not on the choice of a linear space $E$ such that $E\cap H = \emptyset$. Consider the setting described in Remark \ref{ccc0} with $e =d_{n-m,s}$. Note that $W'$ is projectively equivalent to the $(m+1)$-dimensional minimal degree variety $W$ featured in Remark \ref{ccc0}. Let $X\subset W'$ be an integral divisor such that $X\in |h+df|$, upon an identification $W\cong W'$. Since $d\geq (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$, by Remark \ref{ccc0}, $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree $s-1$. If $X$ were a cone, either its vertex is contained in $E$ or is a point on $Y$. In the first case, upon identification with $W$, as in Remark \ref{ccc0}, let $X'=u^{*}X$ be the pullback of $X$ through $u$. The image of $h\cap u^{*}X$ under the morphism $u$ would be a codimension-one linear space in $u(h)\cong E$. However, this is impossible, as the degree of $u(h\cap X)$ is $d-d_{n-m,s}>1$. The second case is not possible either, because the pullback $X'$ would contain the divisor $h$. However, $X'$ is integral because $u$ is an isomorphism outside $h$, and $X'$ cannot coincide with $h$, as $X$ is a divisor of $W$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a divisor $X\in|h+df|$ on the cone over a minimal degree rational curve, then rule out both possible cone vertices.

nodes.name: Existence of a minimal degree smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ with prescribed cohomology
nodes.statement: By \cite{hi, be2} (for the case $n=4$), \cite{be2} (for the case $n=5$) and \cite{be3} (for the case $n\ge 6$), there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that \[ \deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: There is a smooth rational curve of the minimal degree $d_{n-m,s}$ in $H$ with the expected postulation.
conclusions: there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that \[ \deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}. \]

nodes.name: Kodaira dimension $\kappa(X)$ of a projective surface
nodes.statement: (For a given projective surface $X$, denote by $\kappa(X)$ its Kodaira dimension.)

nodes.name: Upper bounds for $h^0(\Oo _X(s))$ on a smooth surface
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 4$, $s\ge 2$ and $d\ge n-1$. Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a smooth, connected and non-degenerate degree $d$ surface. Then: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] If $\kappa (X)\ne -\infty$, then $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le 2+s^2d/2$. \item[(ii)] If $\kappa(X) = -\infty$, $X\ncong \PP^2$ and $X$ is $\PP^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $\pi: X\rightarrow D$ such that the rational fibers have degree one (i.e., $X$ is a scroll), then $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le 1 + (s^2+2s)d/2$. \item[(iii)] We have $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le 1 + (s^2+3s)d/2$ and equality holds if and only if $d=k^2$ for some $k$ such that $\binom{k+2}{2}\ge n+1$, $X\cong \PP^2$ and $X$ is isomorphic to either the degree $k$ Veronese embedding of $\PP^2$ or to an isomorphic linear projection of it. \item[(iv)] Otherwise, if $\omega_X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef, then $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le 1 + (s^2+\frac{3}{2}s)d/2$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Kodaira-dimension-dependent upper bounds for $h^0(\Oo_X(s))$, with equality in the universal bound only for (projected) Veronese surfaces.
assumptions: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a  smooth, connected and non-degenerate degree $d$ surface.
conclusions: If $\kappa(X) = -\infty$, $X\ncong \PP^2$ and $X$ is $\PP^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $\pi: X\rightarrow D$ such that the rational fibers have degree one (i.e., $X$ is a scroll), then $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le 1 + (s^2+2s)d/2$.

We have $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le 1 + (s^2+3s)d/2$ and equality holds if and only if $d=k^2$ for some $k$ such that $\binom{k+2}{2}\ge n+1$, $X\cong \PP^2$ and $X$ is isomorphic to either the degree $k$ Veronese embedding of $\PP^2$ or to an isomorphic linear projection of it.

nodes.name: Proof of the upper bounds for $h^0(\Oo _X(s))$
nodes.statement: Fix a general $C\in |\Oo _X(s)|$. By Bertini's theorem, $C$ is a smooth and connected curve of degree $sd$. By the genus formula, $C$ has genus \[ g = 1 + (s^2d + \omega _X\cdot \Oo _X(s))/2. \] Multiplying by the section $C$ yields the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \to \Oo _X\to \Oo _X(s)\to \Oo _C(s)\to 0. \end{equation} Thus $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le h^0(\Oo _C(s)) +1$, where equality holds if $h^1(\Oo _X)=0$. \\ If $s^2d = \deg (\Oo _C(s)) \le 2g-2$, then this divisor on $C$ is special and Clifford's theorem \cite[pp. 107--108]{acgh} gives \[ h^0(\Oo _C(s)) \le 1 +s^2d/2. \] Whence $h^0(\Oo _X(s))\le 2 +s^2d/2$. From now on, assume $s^2d\ge 2g-1$ (or equivalently, $\Oo _C(s)$ is non-special). Again, by the genus formula, one has \[ \omega _X \cdot \Oo _X(1) <0. \] Note that Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\Oo _C(s)) =s^2d +1-g = \frac{1}{2}(s^2d -s\omega _X\cdot \Oo _X(1))$. Before we proceed, recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$. \begin{quote} {\it Claim.} If $\omega _X \cdot \Oo _X(1) <0$, then $\kappa (X)=-\infty$. \\ {\it Proof of the Claim.} Assume on the contrary that $\kappa (X)\ge 0$. Let $X'$ be the minimal model of $X$ and $\phi: X\to X'$ be the corresponding morphism. Since $\kappa (X') =\kappa (X)\ge 0$, $\omega _{X'}$ is nef. We have $\omega _X \cong \phi^\ast\omega _{X'} +E$, where $E$ is an effective divisor and $E = 0$ if and only if $X$ is minimal. Since $\phi^\ast\omega _{X'}$ is nef and $\Oo_X(1)$ is effective, we derive \[ ( \phi^\ast \omega _{X'} +E)\cdot \Oo _X(1)\ge 0, \] which is a contradiction. \end{quote} The {\it Claim} shows that the Kodaira dimension of $X$ is $\kappa (X) = -\infty$, and statement (i) is proven. We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\Ll$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\Ll$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\Ll) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \  \Ll +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where  $\Ll +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\Ll +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}. Thus we have the following cases: \begin{itemize} \item $u=1$ and $v=3$. The cone of curves of $X$ has an {\it extremal ray} of {\it length} $3 =\dim X +1$; see \cite{matsuki} for these notions. This implies $X\cong \PP^2$ and $\Oo _X(1)$ is the generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Since $n\ge 4$, $X$ is embedded as described in the statement. \item $u=1$ and $v=2$. Since $\Ll+\frac{1}{2}\omega _X$ is nef, so is the line bundle $2\Ll+\omega _X$. In this case, there exists a curve $C\subset X$ such that $C\cdot (2\Ll+\omega _X) =0$. By \cite[Theorem 1-4-8]{matsuki}, $X$ is a $\PP^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $D$, $\pi: X\to D$, and $\Ll\cong\Oo _X(1)$ has degree $1$ on each fiber $C$ of $\pi$. In such a case, $\omega _X(2)$ is nef and hence $\omega_X\cdot \Oo_X(1) \geq -2$. This proves statement (ii). \\ \item $u\ge 2$ or $v=1$. Then $\omega _X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef and therefore $\omega_X\cdot \Oo_X(1)\geq -3/2$. In this case, we obtain (iv). \end{itemize} In conclusion, the discussion above yields $\omega_X\cdot \Oo_X(1)\geq -3$ for all $X$, with equality if and only if $X\cong \PP^2$. This proves statement (iii).
nodes.statement_short: Cut with a general $C\in|\Oo_X(s)|$, split into special (Clifford) and non-special cases, then run the Kawamata Rationality Theorem case-by-case on the nef-value.

nodes.name: Claim: $\omega _X \cdot \Oo _X(1) <0$ forces $\kappa (X)=-\infty$
nodes.statement: If $\omega _X \cdot \Oo _X(1) <0$, then $\kappa (X)=-\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of the Claim on the Kodaira dimension
nodes.statement: Assume on the contrary that $\kappa (X)\ge 0$. Let $X'$ be the minimal model of $X$ and $\phi: X\to X'$ be the corresponding morphism. Since $\kappa (X') =\kappa (X)\ge 0$, $\omega _{X'}$ is nef. We have $\omega _X \cong \phi^\ast\omega _{X'} +E$, where $E$ is an effective divisor and $E = 0$ if and only if $X$ is minimal. Since $\phi^\ast\omega _{X'}$ is nef and $\Oo_X(1)$ is effective, we derive \[ ( \phi^\ast \omega _{X'} +E)\cdot \Oo _X(1)\ge 0, \] which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: if $\kappa(X)\ge0$ the minimal model makes $\omega_X$ a sum of a nef pullback and an effective divisor, forcing $\omega_X\cdot\Oo_X(1)\ge0$.

nodes.name: Nef line bundle
nodes.statement: recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$.
nodes.origin_citation: standard notion; cf. Beltrametti & Schenzel-Brodmann, Matsuki 2002
nodes.genus: a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$
differentia: $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$

nodes.name: Nef-value $\tau(\Ll)$
nodes.statement: For each ample line bundle $\Ll$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\Ll$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\Ll) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \  \Ll +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where  $\Ll +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$.
differentia: For each ample line bundle $\Ll$ on $X$

nodes.name: Kawamata Rationality Theorem (smooth surface case)
nodes.statement: We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\Ll$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\Ll$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\Ll) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \  \Ll +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where  $\Ll +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\Ll +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}.
nodes.statement_short: The nef-value of an ample bundle on a smooth surface with non-nef canonical class is rational with denominator in $\{1,2,3\}$, and is attained.
nodes.origin_citation: Kawamata; Brodmann & Schenzel, Theorem 1.5.2; Matsuki 2002, Corollary 1-2-15
assumptions: Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef.
For each ample line bundle $\Ll$ on $X$
conclusions: the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$

nodes.name: Section exact sequence of $\Oo _X(s)$ along $C$
nodes.statement: 0 \to \Oo _X\to \Oo _X(s)\to \Oo _C(s)\to 0.

nodes.name: Consequence for $d_{n,s+1,2}$ via projected Veronese surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $n, s$ be integers as in the assumptions of Theorem \ref{ma1}, and let $k$ be an integer. Assume $\binom{n+s}{n} \le 1+(s^2+3s)k^2/2$. From the ideal sheaf exact sequence and Theorem \ref{ma1} (iii), one has \[ h^1(\Ii _X(s)) \ge 1+(s^2+3s)k^2/2 -\binom{n+s}{n}, \] for any isomorphic projection $X\subset \PP^n$ of the degree $k$ Veronese embedding of $\PP^2$. Assuming the existence of such an $X$ with the additional property that the latter inequality is an equality, one obtains $h^0(\Ii_X(s))=0$. Thus $d_{n,s+1,2} \le \deg(X) = k^2$.
nodes.statement_short: If the $h^1$ bound from Theorem (iii) is sharp for a projected Veronese surface, then $d_{n,s+1,2}\le k^2$.

nodes.name: Cohomology of general projections of Veronese surfaces (Ballico--Ellia)
nodes.statement: Let $d \ge 2$ and $n\ge 5$. Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a general isomorphic linear projection of a degree $k$ Veronese embedding $Y\subset \PP^N$ of $\PP^2$, where $N= (k^2+3k)/2$. Then \[ h^0(\Ii _X(2)) = \max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}, \] \[ \mbox{ and } h^1(\Ii _X(2)) =  \max \left\{0,\binom{2k+2}{2}-\binom{n+2}{2} \right\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: A general projection of a degree $k$ Veronese surface has the expected $h^0$ and $h^1$ of quadrics.
assumptions: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a general isomorphic linear projection of a degree $k$ Veronese embedding $Y\subset \PP^N$ of $\PP^2$, where $N= (k^2+3k)/2$.

nodes.name: Bound $d_{n,3,2} \le (n+1)^2/4$ for odd $n\ge5$
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 5$ be an odd integer. Then $d_{n,3,2} \le (n+1)^2/4$.

nodes.name: Proof of the bound $d_{n,3,2} \le (n+1)^2/4$
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a general linear projection of the degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese embedding of $\PP^2$. By Proposition \ref{be1}, we have \[ h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{n+3}{2}\right\}=0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit the projected degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese surface and check $h^0(\Ii_X(2))=0$ via the previous proposition.

nodes.name: Question: cohomology of projected Veronese surfaces for all $s$
nodes.statement: Fix integers $d \ge 2, s\ge 3$, and $n\ge 5$. Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a general isomorphic linear projection of a degree $k$ Veronese embedding $Y\subset \PP^N$ of $\PP^2$, where $N= (k^2+3k)/2$. Is it true that \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s)) = \max \left\{0,\binom{n+s}{n} -\binom{sk+2}{2}\right\}, \] \[ \mbox{ and } h^1(\Ii _X(s)) =  \max \left\{0,\binom{sk+2}{2}-\binom{n+s}{n} \right\}? \]

nodes.name: Summary bound for quadrics through surfaces, even $n\ge6$
nodes.statement: Let $n\ge 6$ be even. Then $h^0(\Ii _X(2)) \ge \binom{n+2}{2} - 1 - 5d$ for all smooth connected and non-degenerate surfaces of degree $d$. Moreover, there exists a smooth and connected surface $X\subset \PP^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n^2/4$, $h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =0$, and $X\cong \PP^2$.
nodes.statement_short: For even $n\ge6$ every smooth surface lies on at least $\binom{n+2}{2}-1-5d$ quadrics, and a projected Veronese surface of degree $n^2/4$ lies on none.
conclusions: $h^0(\Ii _X(2)) \ge \binom{n+2}{2} - 1 - 5d$ for all smooth connected and non-degenerate surfaces of degree $d$
Moreover, there exists a smooth and connected surface $X\subset \PP^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n^2/4$, $h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =0$, and $X\cong \PP^2$.

nodes.name: Proof of the summary bound for even $n\ge6$
nodes.statement: The first part is statement (iii) of Theorem \ref{ma1}. By Proposition \ref{be1}, the general isomorphic linear projection of the degree $k$ Veronese surface has \[ h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}. \] Thus the choice $k = n/2$ establishes the second statement.
nodes.statement_short: Quote statement (iii) of the theorem, then specialize the projected Veronese formula at $k=n/2$.

nodes.name: Bound on $h^0(\Ii _{X}(2))$ via sectional genus
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate surface of sectional genus $g$ and degree $d$. Then $h^0(\Ii _{X}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g$.
assumptions: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be an integral and non-degenerate surface of sectional genus $g$ and degree $d$.

nodes.name: Proof of the sectional genus bound on $h^0(\Ii _{X}(2))$
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \PP^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \longrightarrow \Ii _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \Ii _X(s)\longrightarrow \Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\Oo_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. Thus \[ h^0(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g. \] By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\Ii _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to a general hyperplane, bound quadrics through the section by Riemann-Roch, then lift through the ideal sheaf sequence.

nodes.name: Hyperplane restriction sequence for a surface ideal sheaf
nodes.statement: 0 \longrightarrow \Ii _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \Ii _X(s)\longrightarrow \Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0.

nodes.name: Cohomological facts on surfaces of almost-minimal degree
nodes.statement: A complete classification of surfaces of almost-minimal degree, i.e., all integral and non-degenerate surfaces $X\subset \PP^n$ such that $\deg (X) =n$ is known; see, e.g., \cite{hsv, park1}. Let $H\subset \PP^n$ be a general hyperplane. Since $C=X\cap H$ is a degree $n$ integral curve spanning $H$, there are two possibilities: either $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a(C) =1$ or $C$ is a smooth rational curve. In the latter case, $X$ may have only finitely many singular points. \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] $C$ is arithmetically Cohen-Macaulay with $p_a({C}) =1$. The surface $X$ is linearly normal of degree $\deg(X)\geq 2p_a(C)+1$. Note that this case may occur for all $n$: take a cone over a linearly normal elliptic curve $C\subset \PP^{n-1}$. \item[(ii)] $C$ is a smooth rational curve. Thus $h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1$, $h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(2)) =0$, and so $h^0(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(2)) = \binom{n+1}{2} -2n-1$. It is clear that \[ h^1(\Ii _X(1)) \le h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(1)) =1. \] From (\ref{eqw1}), we derive $\binom{n+1}{2} -2n-2\le h^0(\Ii _X(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} -2n-1$. Now, if $X$ is smooth and $X\cap H$ is rational, then the classification of surfaces gives that $X$ is rational. Thus $h^1(\Oo _X)=0$. A standard exact sequence gives $h^0(\Oo _X(1)) =h^0(\Oo _{X\cap H}(1)) +1=n+2$ and $h^0(\Oo _X(2))= h^0(\Oo _{X\cap H}(2)) +h^0(\Oo _X(1)) = 3n+3$. Thus $h^1(\Ii _X(1)) =1$ and so $X$ is not linearly normal. Let $X'\subset \PP^{n+1}$ be a smooth surface such that $X$ is an isomorphic linear projection of $X'$ from some $p\in \PP^{n+1}$ with $p$ not contained in the secant variety of $X'$. Thus $\deg(X') = n$ and since $X'\subset \PP^{n+1}$, it is either a minimal degree surface scroll or (when $n=4$) the Veronese surface. In any case, one knows the minimal free resolution of $X'$, and it follows that $X'$ has property $K_2$, following Alzati and Russo \cite[Definition 3.1]{ar}. By \cite[Theorem 3.2 or Corollary 3.3]{ar}, we have $h^1(\Ii _X(2))=0$. Hence $h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =\binom{n+2}{2} -3n-3$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $\deg X=n$ the general hyperplane section is either aCM of genus 1 or rational; in the rational case $h^1(\Ii_X(2))=0$ and $h^0(\Ii_X(2))=\binom{n+2}{2}-3n-3$.

nodes.name: Introduce $\delta$ and restate the goal
nodes.statement: Let \[ \delta = \left\lceil \left(\binom{n+s-1}{n}-1\right)/(s-1)\right\rceil. \] We show that $d_{n,s} = \delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Name the candidate value $\delta$ and reduce to proving $d_{n,s}=\delta$.

nodes.name: Upper bound from general maximal rank rational curves
nodes.statement: For any integer $d\ge n$, the set $H(d,0;n)$ of all smooth and non-degenerate degree $d$ rational curves $X\subset \PP^n$ has the structure of a smooth and integral algebraic variety, whose general point $X$ has {\it maximal rank}: hence $h^0(\Ii _X(t)) =0$ for some $t\in \NN$ if and only if $d t+1\geq h^0(\Oo_{\PP^n}(t))$, i.e., whenever it is possible for the restriction morphism to be injective; see \cite{hi, be3}. Thus a general $X\in H(d,0;n)$ satisfies \[ h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0 \ \ \mbox{ if and only if } \ \ (s-1)d+1\ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] This implies that $d_{n,s}\leq \delta$, as we have a (rational) integral curve of degree $\delta$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply maximal rank of the general rational curve to produce a member of $\Aa(n,s)$ of degree $\delta$, giving $d_{n,s}\le\delta$.

nodes.name: Set up the converse inequality on an arbitrary integral curve
nodes.statement: For the converse inequality, consider any integral curve $Y\subset \PP^n$ such that $h^0(\Ii _Y(s-1)) =0$, and let $k = \deg (Y)$. Since $h^0(\Ii _Y(s-1)) =0$, we have $h^0(\Oo _Y(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$. Since $Y$ is an integral curve (of arbitrary arithmetic genus), elementary considerations give \[ h^0(L) \le \deg (L)+1, \] for an arbitrary line bundle $L$ on $Y$.
nodes.statement_short: For any $Y\in\Aa(n,s)$ combine $h^0(\Oo_Y(s-1))\ge\binom{n+s-1}{n}$ with $h^0(L)\le\deg(L)+1$.

nodes.name: Conclude $d_{n,s} \ge \delta$
nodes.statement: Thus \[ \deg(\Oo_Y(s-1))+1 = (s-1)k+1 \ge h^0(\Oo_Y(s-1))\geq \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Taking the minimum, the latter inequality implies $d_{n,s}\geq \delta$, which completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Take the minimum over $Y$ to get the reverse inequality $d_{n,s}\ge\delta$.

nodes.name: Non-special case via Riemann-Roch
nodes.statement: Since $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1))=0$, Riemann-Roch shows that the statement is true if $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: When $h^1(\Oo_X(s-1))=0$ the bound is immediate from Riemann-Roch.

nodes.name: Special case: apply Clifford's theorem
nodes.statement: Otherwise, assume $h^1(\Oo _X(s-1)) >0$. Since $h^0(\Oo _X(s-1)) \ge \binom{n+s-1}{n}$, Clifford's theorem gives $(s-1)d_{n,s} \ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$.
nodes.statement_short: In the special case Clifford's theorem forces $(s-1)d_{n,s}\ge 2\binom{n+s-1}{n}-2$.

nodes.name: Contradiction with $s\ge3$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{i1}, we have \[ (s-1)(d_{n,s} -1)+2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \] Altogether, they give $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, contradicting the assumption $s\ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with the value of $d_{n,s}$ to reach $\binom{n+s-1}{n}\le s-1$, absurd for $s\ge3$.

nodes.name: Contradiction hypothesis and reduction to an inequality
nodes.statement: By contradiction, assume $d_{n,s} \le n+s-3$. By Proposition \ref{i1}, in order to obtain a contradiction, it is enough to show \[ (s-1)(n+s-3) +2 \le \binom{n+s-1}{n}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume $d_{n,s}\le n+s-3$ and reduce to a binomial inequality.

nodes.name: Introduce the auxiliary function $\phi (n,s)$
nodes.statement: Let $\phi (n,s) = \binom{n+s-1}{n} - (s-1)(n+s-3)-2$. This function is non-negative in the desired range.
nodes.statement_short: Encode the inequality as non-negativity of $\phi(n,s)$.

nodes.name: Base case $n=3$
nodes.statement: Indeed, consider \[ \phi (3,s) = (s+2)(s+1)s/6 -s(s-1)-2. \] It is clear this is non-negative for all $s\ge 3$.
nodes.statement_short: Check $\phi(3,s)\ge0$ for all $s\ge3$.

nodes.name: Increment in $n$ and conclusion
nodes.statement: Moreover: \[ \phi (n+1,s) -\phi (n,s) =\binom{n+s-2}{n} -s+1 \ge 0, \ \ \mbox{ for all } \ \ s\ge 3, \] which leads to a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\phi$ is non-decreasing in $n$, completing the contradiction.

nodes.name: Count sections on a general hyperplane
nodes.statement: Fix a general hyperplane $H\subset \PP^n$. Note that $h^0(H,\Ii _{X\cap H}(s)) =\binom{n+s-1}{n-1}-\deg (X)+h^1(H,\Ii _{X\cap H}(s))$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $h^0$ of the degree $s$ forms on $H$ vanishing on $X\cap H$.

nodes.name: Identify $h^1(\Oo _X(t))$ with $h^2(\Ii _X(t))$
nodes.statement: Since $h^1(\Oo _X(t)) =h^2(\Ii _X(t))$ for all $t\in \mathbb Z$, in order to conclude it is sufficient to use the long exact sequence in cohomology of the exact sequence
nodes.statement_short: Translate the $\Oo_X$ terms into $\Ii_X$ terms.

nodes.name: Run the long exact sequence of the restriction sequence
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} 0\to \Ii _X(s-1)\to \Ii _X(s)\to \Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s)\to 0, \end{equation} along with the assumption $h^0(\Ii _X(s-1)) =0$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude from the long exact sequence together with $h^0(\Ii_X(s-1))=0$.

nodes.name: Degree as an intersection product in the Chow ring
nodes.statement: Since $u$ is a morphism birational onto its image, $\deg (W)= (h+ef)^{m+1}$, where the latter integer is the intersection product in the Chow ring of $T$ of $m+1$ copies of the divisor $h+ef$ defining the morphism.
nodes.statement_short: Birationality of $u$ turns $\deg W$ into the self-intersection $(h+ef)^{m+1}$.

nodes.name: Expand using $f^2=0$
nodes.statement: Since any two different fibers of $\pi$ are disjoint, the class $f^2$ in the Chow ring is zero. Thus $(h+ef)^{m+1} = h^{m+1} +(m+1)eh^mf$.
nodes.statement_short: Only two terms survive because $f^2=0$.

nodes.name: Compute $h^m f = 1$ on a fiber
nodes.statement: Fix a fiber $F\in |f|$ of $\pi$. Since $h_{|F}$ is the degree one line bundle on $F$ and $F\cong \PP^{m}$, we have $h^{m}f =1$ and hence $(m+1)eh^{m}f =(m+1)e$.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction to a fiber $\PP^m$ gives $h^mf=1$.

nodes.name: Case $m=1$: rational ruled surface
nodes.statement: If $m=1$, $T$ is a rational ruled surface. The normal bundle of $h$ has degree $h^2=-e$. Hence the conclusion follows for $m=1$.
nodes.statement_short: For $m=1$ the normal bundle gives $h^2=-e$ directly.

nodes.name: Case $m\ge2$: normal bundle and induction
nodes.statement: Assume $m\ge 2$. Since $h \cong \PP^1\times \PP^{m-1}$, we have $\mathrm{Pic}(h)\cong \ZZ^2$. As generators of the lattice $\mathrm{Pic}(h)$, we take the pullbacks of hyperplane classes of the factors through the projections $\pi _1: h\to \PP^1$ and $\pi _2: h\to \PP^{m-1}$, i.e., $\Oo _h(1,0) = \pi _1^\ast (\Oo_{\PP^1}(1))$ and $\Oo _h(0,1) = \pi _2^\ast (\Oo _{\PP^{m-1}}(1))$. By definition, the restriction $h_{|h}$ is the normal bundle of $h$ in $T$ and hence $h_{|h} \cong \Oo _h(-e,1)$, by induction on $m$ and using standard exact sequences on normal bundles. Thus $h^{m+1} = h^m|_{h} = -me$, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: For $m\ge2$ identify $h_{|h}\cong\Oo_h(-e,1)$ by induction and get $h^{m+1}=-me$.

nodes.name: Choose complementary linear subspaces $H$ and $E$
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \PP^n$ be a linear subspace with $\dim H = n-m$. Take a linear subspace $E\subset \PP^n$ such that $\dim E =m-1$ and $E\cap H=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix disjoint linear subspaces of dimensions $n-m$ and $m-1$.

nodes.name: Invoke the existence of a minimal degree rational curve in $H$
nodes.statement: By \cite{hi, be2} (for the case $n=4$), \cite{be2} (for the case $n=5$) and \cite{be3} (for the case $n\ge 6$), there exists a smooth rational curve $Y\subset H$ such that \[ \deg (Y) =d_{n-m,s},\ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s-1)) =0,\ \mbox{and} \ \ h^0(H,\Ii _{Y,H}(s)) = \binom{n+s-m}{n-m} -d_{n-m,s}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Quote the known existence of a smooth rational curve of degree $d_{n-m,s}$ with expected postulation.

nodes.name: Build the cone $W'$ and the divisor $X\in |h+df|$
nodes.statement: Let $W'$ be the cone with vertex $E$ and such a curve $Y\subset H$ as its base. Up to a projective transformation, the projective variety depends only on $Y$, and not on the choice of a linear space $E$ such that $E\cap H = \emptyset$. Consider the setting described in Remark \ref{ccc0} with $e =d_{n-m,s}$. Note that $W'$ is projectively equivalent to the $(m+1)$-dimensional minimal degree variety $W$ featured in Remark \ref{ccc0}. Let $X\subset W'$ be an integral divisor such that $X\in |h+df|$, upon an identification $W\cong W'$. Since $d\geq (s-1)d_{n-m,s}+1$, by Remark \ref{ccc0}, $X$ is not contained in any hypersurface of degree $s-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Cone over $Y$ with vertex $E$, identify it with $W$, and take $X\in|h+df|$, which lies on no degree $s-1$ hypersurface.

nodes.name: Rule out a vertex contained in $E$
nodes.statement: If $X$ were a cone, either its vertex is contained in $E$ or is a point on $Y$. In the first case, upon identification with $W$, as in Remark \ref{ccc0}, let $X'=u^{*}X$ be the pullback of $X$ through $u$. The image of $h\cap u^{*}X$ under the morphism $u$ would be a codimension-one linear space in $u(h)\cong E$. However, this is impossible, as the degree of $u(h\cap X)$ is $d-d_{n-m,s}>1$.
nodes.statement_short: A vertex inside $E$ would force a linear image of too small degree.

nodes.name: Rule out a vertex on $Y$
nodes.statement: The second case is not possible either, because the pullback $X'$ would contain the divisor $h$. However, $X'$ is integral because $u$ is an isomorphism outside $h$, and $X'$ cannot coincide with $h$, as $X$ is a divisor of $W$.
nodes.statement_short: A vertex on $Y$ would force $X'$ to contain $h$, contradicting integrality.

nodes.name: Cut with a general $C\in |\Oo _X(s)|$ and compute its genus
nodes.statement: Fix a general $C\in |\Oo _X(s)|$. By Bertini's theorem, $C$ is a smooth and connected curve of degree $sd$. By the genus formula, $C$ has genus \[ g = 1 + (s^2d + \omega _X\cdot \Oo _X(s))/2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Bertini plus the genus formula for a general member of $|\Oo_X(s)|$.

nodes.name: Exact sequence and the bound $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le h^0(\Oo _C(s)) +1$
nodes.statement: Multiplying by the section $C$ yields the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \to \Oo _X\to \Oo _X(s)\to \Oo _C(s)\to 0. \end{equation} Thus $h^0(\Oo _X(s)) \le h^0(\Oo _C(s)) +1$, where equality holds if $h^1(\Oo _X)=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the surface count to a curve count, losing at most one.

nodes.name: Special case: Clifford's theorem gives statement (i)
nodes.statement: If $s^2d = \deg (\Oo _C(s)) \le 2g-2$, then this divisor on $C$ is special and Clifford's theorem \cite[pp. 107--108]{acgh} gives \[ h^0(\Oo _C(s)) \le 1 +s^2d/2. \] Whence $h^0(\Oo _X(s))\le 2 +s^2d/2$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\Oo_C(s)$ is special, Clifford yields $h^0(\Oo_X(s))\le 2+s^2d/2$.

nodes.name: Non-special case: $\omega _X \cdot \Oo _X(1) <0$
nodes.statement: From now on, assume $s^2d\ge 2g-1$ (or equivalently, $\Oo _C(s)$ is non-special). Again, by the genus formula, one has \[ \omega _X \cdot \Oo _X(1) <0. \] Note that Riemann-Roch gives $h^0(\Oo _C(s)) =s^2d +1-g = \frac{1}{2}(s^2d -s\omega _X\cdot \Oo _X(1))$.
nodes.statement_short: In the non-special case the genus formula forces $\omega_X\cdot\Oo_X(1)<0$ and Riemann-Roch computes $h^0(\Oo_C(s))$.

nodes.name: Recall the notion of a nef line bundle
nodes.statement: Before we proceed, recall that a line bundle $\mathcal L$ on a projective variety $X$ of dimension $\ge 2$ is said to be \emph{nef} if $\mathcal L \cdot C\ge 0$, for every algebraic curve $C\subset X$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall nefness, needed for the Mori-theoretic input.

nodes.name: The Claim yields $\kappa (X) = -\infty$ and statement (i)
nodes.statement: The {\it Claim} shows that the Kodaira dimension of $X$ is $\kappa (X) = -\infty$, and statement (i) is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Claim to conclude $\kappa(X)=-\infty$, proving (i).

nodes.name: Recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem and the nef-value
nodes.statement: We recall the Kawamata Rationality Theorem in the case of smooth surfaces. Let $X$ be a smooth projective surface such that $\omega _X$ is {\it not} nef. For each ample line bundle $\Ll$ on $X$, the {\it nef-value} $\tau$ of $\Ll$ with respect to $\omega_X$ is defined as \[ \tau(\Ll) = \sup \lbrace t>0 \ | \  \Ll +t\omega _X \mbox{ is nef} \rbrace, \] where  $\Ll +t\omega _X$ is viewed as a functional on the cone of curves depending on a parameter $t$. The aforementioned theorem states that the real number $\tau$ is rational, $\tau = u/v$, where $u$ is a positive integer and $v\in \{1,2,3\}$; see, e.g., \cite[Theorem 1.5.2]{bs}, \cite[Corollary 1-2-15]{matsuki}. Moreover, $\Ll +\tau \omega_X$ is nef \cite[Lemma 1.5.5]{bs}, \cite[Theorem 1-2-14]{matsuki}. Thus we have the following cases:
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the nef-value $\tau=u/v$ with $v\in\{1,2,3\}$ and split into cases on $(u,v)$.

nodes.name: Case $u=1$, $v=3$: $X\cong \PP^2$
nodes.statement: $u=1$ and $v=3$. The cone of curves of $X$ has an {\it extremal ray} of {\it length} $3 =\dim X +1$; see \cite{matsuki} for these notions. This implies $X\cong \PP^2$ and $\Oo _X(1)$ is the generator of $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$. Since $n\ge 4$, $X$ is embedded as described in the statement.
nodes.statement_short: An extremal ray of length 3 forces $X\cong\PP^2$ embedded by a Veronese-type system.

nodes.name: Case $u=1$, $v=2$: scroll, giving statement (ii)
nodes.statement: $u=1$ and $v=2$. Since $\Ll+\frac{1}{2}\omega _X$ is nef, so is the line bundle $2\Ll+\omega _X$. In this case, there exists a curve $C\subset X$ such that $C\cdot (2\Ll+\omega _X) =0$. By \cite[Theorem 1-4-8]{matsuki}, $X$ is a $\PP^1$-bundle over a smooth curve $D$, $\pi: X\to D$, and $\Ll\cong\Oo _X(1)$ has degree $1$ on each fiber $C$ of $\pi$. In such a case, $\omega _X(2)$ is nef and hence $\omega_X\cdot \Oo_X(1) \geq -2$. This proves statement (ii).
nodes.statement_short: Here $X$ is a scroll and $\omega_X\cdot\Oo_X(1)\ge-2$, giving (ii).

nodes.name: Case $u\ge2$ or $v=1$: statement (iv)
nodes.statement: $u\ge 2$ or $v=1$. Then $\omega _X^{\otimes 2}(3)$ is nef and therefore $\omega_X\cdot \Oo_X(1)\geq -3/2$. In this case, we obtain (iv).
nodes.statement_short: Remaining cases give $\omega_X\cdot\Oo_X(1)\ge-3/2$, hence (iv).

nodes.name: Combine the cases to prove statement (iii)
nodes.statement: In conclusion, the discussion above yields $\omega_X\cdot \Oo_X(1)\geq -3$ for all $X$, with equality if and only if $X\cong \PP^2$. This proves statement (iii).
nodes.statement_short: The uniform bound $\omega_X\cdot\Oo_X(1)\ge-3$, with equality only for $\PP^2$, gives (iii).

nodes.name: Assume $\kappa (X)\ge 0$ for contradiction
nodes.statement: Assume on the contrary that $\kappa (X)\ge 0$.

nodes.name: Pass to the minimal model and decompose $\omega _X$
nodes.statement: Let $X'$ be the minimal model of $X$ and $\phi: X\to X'$ be the corresponding morphism. Since $\kappa (X') =\kappa (X)\ge 0$, $\omega _{X'}$ is nef. We have $\omega _X \cong \phi^\ast\omega _{X'} +E$, where $E$ is an effective divisor and $E = 0$ if and only if $X$ is minimal.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\omega_X$ as a nef pullback plus an effective divisor.

nodes.name: Derive the contradiction
nodes.statement: Since $\phi^\ast\omega _{X'}$ is nef and $\Oo_X(1)$ is effective, we derive \[ ( \phi^\ast \omega _{X'} +E)\cdot \Oo _X(1)\ge 0, \] which is a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Both summands pair non-negatively with $\Oo_X(1)$, contradicting negativity.

nodes.name: Choose the projected degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese surface
nodes.statement: Let $X\subset \PP^n$ be a general linear projection of the degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese embedding of $\PP^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the general projection of the degree $(n+1)/2$ Veronese surface.

nodes.name: Compute $h^0(\Ii _X(2)) = 0$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{be1}, we have \[ h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{n+3}{2}\right\}=0. \]
nodes.statement_short: The quadric count vanishes, so this surface lies in $\Aa(n,3,2)$.

nodes.name: First part from statement (iii)
nodes.statement: The first part is statement (iii) of Theorem \ref{ma1}.

nodes.name: Second part from the projected Veronese formula at $k=n/2$
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{be1}, the general isomorphic linear projection of the degree $k$ Veronese surface has \[ h^0(\Ii _X(2)) =\max \left\{0,\binom{n+2}{2} -\binom{2k+2}{2}\right\}. \] Thus the choice $k = n/2$ establishes the second statement.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the projected Veronese formula at $k=n/2$ to get a surface on no quadric.

nodes.name: General hyperplane and the ideal sheaf sequence
nodes.statement: Let $H\subset \PP^n$ be a general hyperplane. Consider the exact sequence \begin{equation} 0 \longrightarrow \Ii _X(s-1)\longrightarrow \Ii _X(s)\longrightarrow \Ii _{X\cap H,H}(s)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to a general hyperplane via the ideal sheaf sequence.

nodes.name: Bound quadrics through the hyperplane section
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is general, $C = X\cap H$ is a smooth curve of degree $d$ and genus $g$. Hence, by Riemann-Roch, $h^0(\Oo_C(2)) \geq 2d+1-g$. Thus \[ h^0(H,\Ii _{X\cap H,H}(2)) \le \binom{n+1}{2} - 2d-1+g. \]
nodes.statement_short: Riemann-Roch on the section bounds the quadrics of $H$ through $C$.

nodes.name: Lift the bound to $X$
nodes.statement: By (\ref{eqw1}) and $h^0(\Ii _X(1)) =0$, the conclusion follows.
